Understanding acute myeloid leukemia

A guide for adults with AML and the people supporting them.

Sources checked September 27, 2026. Educational only. Individual clinician review of this guide is not yet documented. Your leukemia team must personalize testing and treatment.

SymptomsDiagnosisTreatmentUrgent helpQuestions to bring

What AML is and how it can feel

AML is a cancer of blood-forming cells in the bone marrow. Abnormal immature cells can interfere with production of healthy blood cells. Untreated AML can progress quickly and needs prompt specialist evaluation.

Symptoms may include fatigue, weakness, pale skin, fever, infections, and unusual bruising or bleeding. These symptoms also occur in other illnesses. Symptoms alone cannot diagnose leukemia.

Source · National Cancer Institute patient guide

How the diagnosis is established

A complete blood count measures blood cell levels. A blood smear examines their appearance. Bone marrow sampling and flow cytometry help identify the abnormal cells. Chromosome and molecular tests clarify the subtype and help guide treatment.

Ask for a copy of the marrow report and genetic results. Acute promyelocytic leukemia, or APL, is a distinct AML subtype associated with dangerous bleeding and clotting. Suspected APL needs immediate specialist attention and a different treatment approach.

Source · National Cancer Institute patient guide

How treatment decisions are made

There is no single treatment plan for everyone. Leukemia genetics, overall health, organ function, previous treatment, and personal goals shape the recommendation.

Initial treatment

Some people receive intensive chemotherapy. Others receive less-intensive combinations, such as a hypomethylating medicine with venetoclax. Targeted drugs may be appropriate for certain mutations. Less-intensive treatment can still cause serious low blood counts and infections and requires close monitoring.

After a response

Remission is an important response, but does not automatically mean cure. Additional treatment may include consolidation chemotherapy or a donor stem cell transplant in selected patients. Transplant decisions balance relapse risk against treatment risks.

Monitoring and further options

Repeat blood and marrow tests assess response. Measurable residual disease, or MRD, testing looks for small amounts of leukemia using sensitive methods. If AML persists or returns, repeat testing can help guide further therapy. Clinical trials may be worth discussing at diagnosis as well as later.

Source · National Cancer Institute treatment review

When to contact the team urgently

During cancer treatment, fever or other infection symptoms can require urgent care, especially when neutrophils are low. Contact your oncology team immediately for a temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher, or at the lower threshold they gave you. Do not wait until the next appointment. Ask before taking fever-reducing medicines because they can mask infection.

Also report chills, a new cough, painful urination, or redness around a catheter. Keep your team’s daytime and after-hours numbers available.

Call 911 or your local emergency number for severe trouble breathing, uncontrolled bleeding, loss of consciousness, or another life-threatening emergency.

Source · NCI infection and neutropenia guidance

Questions for the care team

  • What exact AML subtype do I have, and has APL been excluded?
  • Which genetic results are available, and which are still pending?
  • What is the goal of the recommended treatment? What alternatives fit my situation?
  • Will I need hospital admission, a caregiver, or frequent clinic visits?
  • How will we prevent and manage infections and bleeding?
  • When will my next marrow test be, and will MRD testing be useful?
  • Should we discuss transplant or a clinical trial now?
  • Which symptoms require an immediate call, and whom do I call overnight?
  • Can we discuss fertility, work, transportation, costs, and emotional support before treatment?

Bring your medication list and a support person if you wish. Ask the team to write down the plan and the next decision point.
